stories.title: Tamil Nadu implements student mental health policy
stories.summary: The Tamil Nadu government has introduced a comprehensive mental health policy for educational institutions to address stress and prevent student suicides. The framework includes the appointment of counsellors, the establishment of dedicated centres, and the promotion of peer support through youth clubs and various government helplines.

Delhi launches Ehsaas 2026 mental health policy for schools
stories.summary: The Delhi government has launched the Ehsaas 2026 policy to integrate emotional support into educational institutions. The framework aims to move beyond isolated counselling sessions by implementing a four-tier system of awareness, early intervention, and specialised care for more than 45 lakh students across the capital.

stories.title: Stanford study tests animated videos for smartphone mindfulness
stories.summary: Researchers at Stanford Medicine and the Heidelberg Institute of Global Health tested whether short, animated videos could reduce compulsive smartphone use. The randomized trial involved 6,061 young adults and aimed to build awareness of problematic scrolling habits. The findings were recently published in Nature Health.

stories.title: Book clubs compared to meditation in new study
stories.summary: Research by The Queen’s Reading Room suggests that participating in a book club provides cognitive benefits comparable to meditation. The charity, which originated as an online book club during the pandemic, arrived at the conclusion after measuring the brain’s electrical activity during group book discussions.

stories.title: IIT Jodhpur study links meditation to drug-like biological effects
stories.summary: Scientists at IIT Jodhpur have identified similarities between biological changes associated with meditation and the effects of 438 different drugs. The study, published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, suggests that meditation may produce measurable biological changes in the body that mirror those targeted by certain pharmaceutical interventions.

stories.summary: The research, titled “Meditation as a Bioactive Intervention: Evidence of Translational Potential via Connectivity Mapping and TMS Neurophysiology,” has been published in the international peer-reviewed journal Frontiers in Human Neuroscience on November 9, 2026. Generally, when we come into contact with something painful or scary, our habitual tendency is to push it away, and to try to

stories.title: Five-minute breathing breaks and stress regulation
stories.summary: Researchers at Stanford University suggest that five minutes of daily breathing exercises may improve mood and help regulate stress responses. A study published in Cell Reports Medicine examined 108 adults to determine if short sessions could impact emotional well-being. The benefits were noted for techniques involving slow exhalation.

stories.title: Akshar Yoga Kendraa aims for one million new teachers
stories.summary: Akshar Yoga Kendraa has launched Bharath Yoga Kranti, an initiative aiming to train one million professional Yoga teachers by 2030. The program offers 1,500 residential scholarships in its first phase, combining Yoga education with skill development and livelihood support. The institution intends to move the practice beyond the studio.

stories.title: Self-compassion research and common misconceptions
stories.summary: Practicing self-compassion is often dismissed as selfish or self-indulgent, according to recent commentary. Research suggests that being kind to oneself is not a self-focused act. The author, who has written on the subject, notes that these common beliefs about the practice are only half-truths.

stories.title: Sleep consistency linked to heart health
stories.summary: A study of 10,000 US adults suggests that consistent sleep schedules may be more closely linked to heart health than total sleep duration. Researchers analyzed six months of tracker data alongside medical records. The study found no significant association between average sleep duration and major cardiovascular conditions.

stories.title: Weighted blankets and sleep in Prader-Willi syndrome
stories.summary: A small clinical trial suggests that weighted blankets may help adults with Prader-Willi syndrome sleep better and experience fewer behavioral problems. The blankets provide deep proprioceptive stimulation, a form of pressure intended to calm the nervous system. Participants also showed lower anxiety and increased muscle mass after two weeks.

stories.title: Vitamin D levels and sleep quality
stories.summary: Higher vitamin D levels were associated with longer and less interrupted sleep in a study of 460 middle-aged and older adults. Researchers at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health analyzed blood tests and wrist-worn sleep data. Vitamin D deficiency was linked to shorter total sleep times.

stories.title: Sleep consistency over duration for heart health
stories.summary: New research suggests that the consistency of a sleep schedule is a more important consideration for heart health than the total time spent in bed. While advice often focuses on achieving eight hours, the regularity of bedtimes and wake times appears to carry more weight for long-term health.

stories.title: Auditory stimulation during sleep and brain fluid flow
stories.summary: Researchers have developed a method to strengthen cerebrospinal fluid flow waves by playing sounds during the peaks of slow brain waves. The study, involving 14 volunteers, combined acoustic stimuli with MRI and EEG measurements. The effect was observed only when sounds were played at the precise moment.

stories.title: Sound sleep and brain health in patients with chronic conditions
stories.summary: A study from the Karolinska Institute found that patients with type 2 diabetes, heart disease, or a history of stroke who slept well had better memory skills than those who slept poorly. Sound sleepers also exhibited greater brain volumes, which are linked to a lower risk of dementia.

stories.title: MIT study finds aging slows brain waste clearance during sleep - NewsBytes
Regular Bedtimes May Reduce CV Risk - Medscape
Irregular sleep patterns and mental health
stories.summary: A study of 23,000 adults suggests that the timing of sleep may be as important for mental health as its duration. Researchers found that varying bedtimes and wake times disrupts biological rhythms. This inconsistency is linked to the regulation of emotions, hormone release, and body temperature.

stories.title: Music listening as a sleep aid at high altitude
stories.summary: A retrospective study of 35 men acclimatizing to high altitude found that adding music listening to standard sleep hygiene education improved sleep quality. The findings suggest that this low-cost intervention may help alleviate insomnia in remote environments. Investigators noted the study was comparative and retrospective in nature.

stories.title: Sleep consistency and mental health symptoms
stories.summary: Research published in Scientific Reports suggests that keeping sleep hours consistent is associated with less severe symptoms of depression and anxiety. Analysts studied wearable data from 23,000 adults. The habit of maintaining a regular schedule may require no extra time, according to the study authors.

stories.title: Sleep timing shifts and mental health
stories.summary: A study of nearly 23,000 adults using Oura Rings explored how day-to-day changes in sleep timing relate to depression, anxiety, and loneliness. The research suggests that shifting bedtimes and weekend wake times may affect mental health symptoms, moving the focus beyond the standard measure of sleep duration.

stories.title: AJ Odudu on bodyweight training
stories.summary: TV presenter AJ Odudu has shared her approach to maintaining strength through bodyweight exercises such as push-ups and squats. Before participating in reality television, she noted that she relied on these movements for training. She expressed optimism about fitting in sessions while away from her usual gym.

stories.title: Monica Galetti on strength training and routine
stories.summary: MasterChef judge Monica Galetti maintains her fitness through weight training and NEAT movement. She attends small-group gym sessions to manage stress and stay independent. She describes her workout routine as an escape from the demands of her professional life in the kitchen.

stories.title: Andie MacDowell on fitness and strength
stories.summary: Actor Andie MacDowell attributes her physical strength to a routine of weight training, walking, and rebounding. She describes exercise as an essential part of her daily life and mental well-being. She has focused on maintaining her health and strength throughout her career.

stories.title: Blood flow restriction training for cyclists yields mixed results
stories.summary: Restricting blood flow to the legs during cycling sprints aims to improve power and endurance, but research remains divided. While some studies report performance gains, others find only increased physiological stress without clear advantages over standard training. The method makes recovery more demanding, if not necessarily more effective.

stories.title: Study challenges muscle loss assumptions for GLP-1 users
stories.summary: Conventional advice suggests resistance training is essential for GLP-1 drug users to prevent muscle loss. New Australian research indicates the relationship between weight-loss medication and muscle preservation is more nuanced than standard gym-or-lose-muscle warnings suggest. Lifting weights remains recommended, but the underlying mechanics are being re-evaluated.

stories.title: Strength training recommended for muscle health in elderly
stories.summary: New findings suggest that strength training is crucial for maintaining muscle health in older adults. While walking is a common habit, experts are urging the elderly to incorporate resistance exercises, noting that combining both activities provides greater benefits for long-term health than walking alone.

stories.title: Resistance training during pregnancy remains under-researched
stories.summary: A 2026 review of 117 studies identified significant gaps in research regarding resistance training during pregnancy. While a small 2025 study reported reassuring physiological responses among experienced lifters, evidence remains limited. Clinically guided strength training is increasingly discussed as a way to address common exercise misconceptions.

stories.title: Weight training shows limited muscle preservation for GLP-1 users
stories.summary: Experts recommend that patients taking GLP-1 drugs like Zepbound or Mounjaro lift weights to maintain strength. However, a study of 120 adults found that weight training preserved little muscle mass during nine months of treatment. The drugs continue to be widely prescribed for weight loss.

stories.title: Weighted vests marketed as simple fitness tools for older adults
stories.summary: Personal trainers are recommending weighted vests to older clients to add challenge to walking and bodyweight exercises. The vests are marketed as a way to increase effort and improve balance, though they are essentially just wearable weights designed to make everyday movement feel more rewarding.

Tai Chi linked to improved bone density in new research
stories.summary: A review published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine links regular Tai Chi practice to improved bone density markers in patients with osteopenia or osteoporosis. The 3,000-year-old exercise is presented as a way to support bone health and reduce the risk of age-related fractures.

stories.title: Fungal toxins found in all tested plant-based foods
stories.summary: Researchers at Cranfield University tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products, including meat alternatives and plant-based milks. Every single item contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin known as a mycotoxin. These compounds naturally contaminate grains and legumes during farming and storage processes.

stories.summary: A fixed breakfast routine may save time, but eating the same morning meal every day may affect your overall nutritional health. Here’s what you need to know. Same oats. Same eggs on toast. Same cup of tea and multigrain biscuits. If your breakfast hasn’t changed in years, you might worry

stories.title: Mushroom coffee lacks clinical evidence for health claims
stories.summary: Influencers promote mushroom coffee as a way to avoid caffeine crashes, yet scientific support is thin. Research on mushroom health benefits is largely limited to labs and animals, and no clinical studies have evaluated the specific effects of mushroom coffee on humans.

stories.title: Olive oil intake associated with cognitive preservation
stories.summary: A two-year observational study found that higher virgin olive oil intake correlates with better cognitive skill preservation and gut microbiome diversity in older adults. Because the study is observational, it does not prove that olive oil prevents dementia or that microbiome changes directly protect the brain.

stories.title: Gut bacteria identified as source of foul-smelling gas
stories.summary: The smell of flatulence is caused by sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria during digestion. A healthy person produces gas 14 to 20 times daily. Scientists note that while some foods increase odor, the volume of gas does not necessarily correlate with the strength of the smell.

stories.title: Broccoli supplement marketed for gut health and inflammation
stories.summary: Kim Kardashian is promoting Broc Shot, a broccoli seed powder supplement claimed to calm inflammation and improve gut health. The product is marketed to those with unpredictable skin conditions like psoriasis, though the reality star's endorsement is part of a sponsored campaign.

Doctor Mike on the limits of sleep tech
stories.summary: Doctor Mikhail Varshavski, known online as Doctor Mike, says sleep is a primary factor in his longevity. While he discusses health with millions of followers, he remains skeptical of most consumer sleep technology. The physician suggests that simple, consistent habits remain the most effective approach to rest.

stories.title: Hemostemix to present longevity treatment data
stories.summary: Hemostemix CEO Thomas Smeenk is presenting peer reviewed findings for the company's VesCell treatment at a virtual investor conference. The company reports that trial participants showed improvements in physical functioning and vitality scores. The presentation aims to highlight the rationale for investing in the company's current equity valuation.

stories.title: Japanese study finds metrics for healthy life expectancy diverge
stories.summary: A study in Population Health Metrics analyzed data from 2001 to 2019 across Japan's 47 prefectures. Researchers found that domestic health indicators and international model-based estimates often produce different results. The findings suggest that current metrics for population well-being are not always interchangeable when measuring healthy life expectancy.

stories.title: Longevity specialist advises against supplement focus
stories.summary: Professor Tzipi Strauss, director of the Sheba Longevity Center, told attendees at a fundraising gala that many supplements result in nothing more than expensive urine. She advised prioritizing diet, sleep, and physical activity over products that promise to extend life. The field of longevity research continues to attract interest.

stories.title: Epigenetic clocks may require regional calibration
stories.summary: Researchers using data from the Costa Rican Longevity and Healthy Aging Study found that calibrating epigenetic clocks to regional populations improves biological age estimates. Conventional clocks are typically trained on broad, heterogeneous datasets. The findings suggest that local dynamics are necessary to accurately measure aging in specific longevity hotspots.

stories.title: Review calls for standardized longevity assessment protocols
stories.summary: A narrative review in Frontiers in Aging identifies a lack of universally adopted frameworks for monitoring biological health in adults aged thirty to eighty. The authors propose an international consensus to standardize assessment protocols. Peer-reviewed publications in the field of human longevity have increased thirty-five-fold since the year 2000.

stories.title: dsm-firmenich frames the gut as a longevity command center
stories.summary: At SupplySide Global 2026, dsm-firmenich presented a booth titled Healthy Longevity 2.0. The company cited a three-year trial where participants using its supplements and light exercise slowed biological aging by three months. The company is currently advising brands on how to translate this science into consumer marketing.

stories.title: Study links long daytime naps to mortality risk
stories.summary: A study of 1,338 older adults published in JAMA Network Open suggests that frequent, long daytime naps are associated with an increased risk of death. Researchers tracked participants for up to 19 years using wrist activity monitors. The findings suggest that prolonged napping may indicate underlying health concerns.

stories.title: A 19-Year Study Reveals a Surprising Link Between Daytime Naps and Longevity - Men's Journal
NMN supplements gain traction among professionals
stories.summary: NMN supplements are increasingly popular among executives seeking improvements in mental clarity and physical endurance. A review by a nutrition coach and dietitian evaluated various products for 2026. The supplements aim to provide cellular support by raising NAD+ levels to assist with healthy aging and focus.

stories.title: Canadians prioritize health but report low scores
stories.summary: According to the 2026 Longevity Preparedness Index, 67 per cent of Canadians rank health as a top priority. However, the report found an average health score of 55 out of 100. The index measures eight areas including finances, community, and daily activities to assess readiness for healthy aging.

stories.title: Exercise guidelines remain difficult for many to meet
stories.summary: Health organizations recommend 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise per week, plus strength training. Fewer than half of Americans meet these targets. While the guidelines are clear, the data suggests that most people are not currently achieving the recommended amount of movement.

stories.title: Tribal healers in Odisha work to preserve medicinal plants
stories.summary: Traditional healers in the Malkangiri district are cultivating medicinal plants to combat the loss of forest species. Nilakantha Krisani has dedicated land to a garden to preserve oral knowledge that has been passed down through generations. The group is now calling for urgent protection of these traditional resources.

stories.title: LSD art study finds abstraction but not creativity
stories.summary: A reanalysis of 1950s experiments shows that artists produced more abstract work while under the influence of LSD. However, blind evaluations by experts found no meaningful increase in overall creativity or aesthetic appeal. The findings suggest that while visual styles may shift, technical skill and creativity remain unchanged.

stories.title: Oregon study reports outcomes for psilocybin therapy
stories.summary: A study of Oregon's state-regulated psilocybin program reports decreased symptoms of mental illness among participants. Dr. Todd Korthuis noted that the findings offer a look at real-world outcomes for the therapy. Oregon was the first state to legalize the use of psilocybin in a supervised clinical setting.

stories.title: Review examines factors in yoga engagement for metabolic health
stories.summary: A systematic review of fifteen studies identifies the barriers and facilitators for using yoga to manage obesity, diabetes, and hypertension. Participants reported physical and psychological benefits, though engagement varied. The researchers synthesized findings into nine themes to better understand how adults utilize yoga for chronic metabolic health.

stories.title: Proposed personalized yoga framework for type 2 diabetes awaits clinical trials
stories.summary: Researchers are exploring whether the Ayurvedic concept of Prakriti can improve outcomes for type 2 diabetes patients. Current clinical practices rely on standardized yoga protocols, which often lead to variable results. The proposed framework aims to move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches, though clinical validation is still pending.

stories.title: India to observe 9th National Naturopathy Day
stories.summary: India will observe the 9th National Naturopathy Day on 18 November 2026 at the Central Research Institute of Yoga and Naturopathy. The event promotes a drug-free system of healthcare using diet, fasting, and massage. The government continues to expand academic and research initiatives for the practice.

stories.title: Psilocybin study suggests improvement for anhedonia in depression
stories.summary: A clinical trial from the University of Colorado Anschutz found that psilocybin may help treat anhedonia, the loss of interest in pleasure, in patients with treatment-resistant depression. Researchers observed improvements eight weeks after treatment. Anhedonia remains one of the most difficult symptoms of depression to address.

stories.title: Clinical considerations for ketamine in treatment-resistant depression
stories.summary: Psychiatric Times outlines clinical guidance for using ketamine to treat depression. Evidence is strongest for major depressive disorder, though experts advise caution and comprehensive suicide-risk management. Dosing protocols remain a subject of active clinical debate, with limited safety data available for higher doses or frequent administration.

stories.title: Blood markers may predict response to psilocybin or ketamine
stories.summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz have identified blood plasma markers that may predict whether a patient will respond to psilocybin or ketamine treatment. The findings were presented at the Neuroscience 2026 meeting. The research aims to help patients who have found no relief elsewhere.

research.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
research.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes.
